name: Stomach ache
summary: Most stomach aches are caused by something minor such as indigestion, trapped wind or a stomach bug, and settle within a few days. Sudden, severe or persistent pain needs to be checked.
redFlags: Sudden, severe stomach pain that does not ease
Stomach pain with vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Black, sticky or bloody poo with stomach pain
Stomach that is hard and very tender to touch
Pain after a recent injury to the stomach area
Collapsing, fainting, or cold, clammy, pale or blue-tinged skin
Severe pain in early pregnancy or a possible pregnancy, especially on one side
urgentFlags: Pain that keeps getting worse or is still there after several hours
Pain that started around the belly button and moved to the lower right side
Stomach pain with a high temperature or feeling hot and shivery
Pain with being unable to keep any fluids down
Pain when passing urine or a need to pee much more often
Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes

commonCauses.title: Indigestion or trapped wind
commonCauses.detail: Often linked to eating, rich or fatty food, or swallowing air, and usually eases on its own.

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug (gastroenteritis)
commonCauses.detail: Cramping pain with diarrhoea or vomiting that usually gets better within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: Cramps and bloating when poo is hard or infrequent.

commonCauses.title: Period pain or other pelvic causes
commonCauses.detail: Low cramping pain linked to the menstrual cycle.

commonCauses.title: Conditions needing treatment
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, appendicitis, gallstones, a stomach ulcer or a urine infection can cause stomach pain.

selfCare: Rest and sip water or other fluids regularly
Eat small, plain meals and stop eating if it makes the pain worse
A hot water bottle or warm (not hot) pad on the stomach may ease cramping
Over-the-counter paracetamol can help, following the pack instructions
Cut down on alcohol, caffeine, fatty and spicy food until you feel better
avoid: Taking ibuprofen or aspirin for stomach pain unless a pharmacist or doctor has advised it, as they can irritate the stomach
Lying flat straight after eating if the pain feels like indigestion
Strong laxatives unless constipation is clearly the cause
seeDoctorIf: The pain keeps coming back
You have lost weight without trying
Your bowel habits have changed for more than a few weeks
You have difficulty swallowing
You are over 55 and have new, persistent indigestion or stomach pain

name: Pain in the lower right side of the stomach
aliases: pain near belly button moving right
summary: Pain low on the right side can come from wind, constipation or the ovaries, but appendicitis is an important cause that needs prompt medical assessment.
redFlags: Pain that suddenly gets much worse or spreads across the whole stomach
Stomach that is hard and very tender to touch
Fainting, collapsing or feeling very unwell with a fast heartbeat
Severe one-sided pain in early pregnancy or a possible pregnancy
Vomiting blood or passing blood with severe pain
urgentFlags: Pain that started around the belly button and moved to the lower right side
Pain that is worse when you move, cough, walk or press on the area
Pain with a high temperature, loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting
Pain that is getting steadily worse over a few hours

commonCauses.title: Trapped wind or constipation
commonCauses.detail: Cramping pain that comes and goes and often eases after passing wind or poo.

commonCauses.title: Appendicitis
commonCauses.detail: Pain often starts near the belly button, moves to the lower right side and gets worse over hours; it usually needs treatment in hospital.

commonCauses.title: Ovary or period-related pain
commonCauses.detail: Pain mid-cycle (ovulation) or from an ovarian cyst can be felt on one side.

commonCauses.title: Gastroenteritis or a urine infection
commonCauses.detail: Stomach bugs and urine or kidney infections can cause pain that is felt on the right side.

selfCare: Rest and sip fluids while you arrange to be checked
Paracetamol can be used for pain, following the pack instructions
Note when the pain started, where it began and whether it has moved, to tell the doctor
avoid: Waiting to see if suspected appendicitis settles on its own
Laxatives, which can be harmful if this is appendicitis
Putting a hot water bottle on the area if appendicitis is possible
seeDoctorIf: Mild pain on the right side keeps coming back
You have one-sided pelvic pain around the same time each month
You have mild pain along with changes in your bowel habits

name: Pain under the right ribs
summary: Pain under the right ribs, especially after a fatty meal, is often linked to the gallbladder. Episodes that come and go should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Severe pain with yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes and a high temperature or shivering
Pain with fainting, confusion or a very fast heartbeat
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
urgentFlags: Pain that lasts longer than 8 hours
Pain with a high temperature or feeling hot and shivery
Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
Dark urine, pale poo or itchy skin with the pain
Pain so bad you cannot find a comfortable position

commonCauses.title: Gallstones
commonCauses.detail: Sudden pain under the right ribs or in the centre of the upper stomach, often after eating, that can last from minutes to hours.

commonCauses.title: Indigestion or trapped wind
commonCauses.detail: Discomfort in the upper stomach, often after eating or with bloating.

commonCauses.title: Muscle strain
commonCauses.detail: Pain that is worse with movement or when pressing on the ribs.

commonCauses.title: Liver problems
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, inflammation of the liver (hepatitis) can cause discomfort in this area.

selfCare: Eat smaller meals and cut down on fatty food
Paracetamol can help with pain, following the pack instructions
Keep a note of when pain happens and what you ate beforehand
avoid: Gallbladder 'flushes' or 'liver cleanses', which are unproven and can cause harm
Drinking alcohol while you have unexplained pain in this area
seeDoctorIf: You have had one or more episodes of pain after eating that have now settled
You have ongoing indigestion or discomfort in the upper stomach
You have lost weight without trying

name: Heartburn and acid reflux
summary: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat. It is very common and often improves with diet and lifestyle changes.
redFlags: Chest pain that spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or comes with breathlessness, sweating or feeling sick
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Black, sticky, tar-like poo
urgentFlags: Food getting stuck when you swallow or pain when swallowing
Being sick repeatedly
Chest discomfort that you are unsure is heartburn

commonCauses.title: Food and drink triggers
commonCauses.detail: Coffee, alcohol, chocolate, fatty or spicy food and large meals can all bring on symptoms.

commonCauses.title: Being overweight
commonCauses.detail: Extra pressure on the stomach makes acid more likely to come up.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Hormone changes and the growing baby often cause heartburn, especially later in pregnancy.

commonCauses.title: Hiatus hernia
commonCauses.detail: Part of the stomach moves up into the chest, which can make reflux worse.

commonCauses.title: Smoking and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: Smoking and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen can make reflux worse.

selfCare: Eat smaller, more frequent meals and avoid eating within 3 to 4 hours of bedtime
Raise the head of your bed by 10 to 20cm so your chest and head are above your waist
Cut down on foods and drinks that trigger your symptoms
Lose weight if you are overweight, and stop smoking
Ask a pharmacist about over-the-counter antacids or acid-reducing medicines, following the pack instructions
avoid: Lying down straight after eating
Tight clothing around the waist
Drinking milk to 'soothe' heartburn, which gives only brief relief
Baking soda remedies, which can be harmful if used often
seeDoctorIf: You have heartburn most days for 3 weeks or more
Pharmacy medicines are not helping
You are 55 or over with new heartburn
You have lost weight without trying
You have heartburn and a feeling of a lump in your throat

name: Indigestion
summary: Indigestion is discomfort or a feeling of fullness in the upper stomach, often after eating. It is common and usually mild.
redFlags: Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Black, sticky, tar-like poo
Sudden severe stomach pain
Chest pain that spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or comes with breathlessness or sweating
urgentFlags: Difficulty swallowing or food getting stuck
Being sick repeatedly
Indigestion with feeling very tired and looking pale, which can be a sign of bleeding

commonCauses.title: Eating habits
commonCauses.detail: Large, rich or fatty meals, eating quickly or eating late at night.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, coffee and smoking
commonCauses.detail: These can irritate the stomach lining.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and aspirin are a common cause.

commonCauses.title: Stomach ulcer or infection
commonCauses.detail: A stomach ulcer or H. pylori infection can cause ongoing indigestion.

selfCare: Eat smaller meals and slow down when eating
Cut down on alcohol, coffee, fatty and spicy food
Stop smoking
Ask a pharmacist about antacids, following the pack instructions
avoid: Taking anti-inflammatory painkillers on an empty stomach
Eating within 3 to 4 hours of going to bed
Relying on antacids for weeks without getting checked
seeDoctorIf: You keep getting indigestion
You are 55 or over and have new indigestion
You have lost weight without trying
Pharmacy medicines have not helped after 2 to 3 weeks

name: Feeling sick (nausea)
summary: Feeling sick is common and usually caused by a stomach bug, motion sickness, pregnancy or medicines. It usually passes within a few days.
redFlags: Chest pain, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with nausea
A sudden, very severe headache with nausea
A stiff neck, sensitivity to light or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it
Severe stomach pain
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Confusion or extreme drowsiness
urgentFlags: Being unable to keep fluids down for more than a day
Signs of dehydration such as passing little or no urine, or dark urine
Nausea in pregnancy that stops you keeping food or drink down
Nausea after a head injury

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug or food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: Often comes with vomiting or diarrhoea and settles within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Morning sickness is common in the first 3 months but can happen at any time of day.

commonCauses.title: Motion sickness
commonCauses.detail: Travelling by car, boat or plane.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol or migraine
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines, a hangover or a migraine can make you feel sick.

commonCauses.title: Indigestion or reflux
commonCauses.detail: Discomfort in the upper stomach with feeling sick, especially after eating.

selfCare: Get plenty of fresh air and rest
Sip small amounts of cold water or other fluids often
Eat small, plain meals such as crackers or toast when you feel able
Ginger may help some people with mild nausea
Ask a pharmacist about medicines for motion sickness if travel is the trigger
avoid: Large, greasy or strongly flavoured meals
Lying down straight after eating
Alcohol
seeDoctorIf: You keep feeling sick for more than a few days
You have also lost weight without trying
You think a medicine is causing it
You keep feeling sick and might be pregnant

name: Vomiting in adults
summary: Vomiting is usually caused by a stomach bug or food poisoning and stops within 1 to 2 days. The main risk is losing too much fluid.
redFlags: Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Green vomit, or vomit that smells like poo
Sudden, severe stomach pain or a hard, swollen stomach
A stiff neck with pain when looking at bright lights
A sudden, severe headache
Confusion, extreme drowsiness or fainting
Signs of sepsis such as cold, blotchy or blue-tinged skin, fast breathing or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it
urgentFlags: Being unable to keep fluids down for 24 hours or more
Signs of dehydration such as dizziness, very dark urine or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Vomiting with bloody diarrhoea
Vomiting for more than 2 days
Vomiting with a weakened immune system, diabetes or kidney disease, or during pregnancy

commonCauses.title: Gastroenteritis (stomach bug)
commonCauses.detail: Often with diarrhoea; usually caused by a virus such as norovirus.

commonCauses.title: Food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: Starts within hours to days of eating contaminated food.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol or medicines
commonCauses.detail: Drinking too much or side effects of some medicines.

commonCauses.title: Migraine or motion sickness
commonCauses.detail: Vomiting can accompany a migraine or travel sickness.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Vomiting is common in early pregnancy.

selfCare: Stay at home and rest
Take small, frequent sips of water; oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy can help replace lost salts
Eat when you feel able, starting with plain foods
Wash your hands often and clean surfaces to avoid spreading a stomach bug
Stay off work or school until 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea
avoid: Fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse
Preparing food for others while unwell
Alcohol
seeDoctorIf: Vomiting keeps coming back over several weeks
You have lost weight without trying
You think a medicine is causing it

name: Diarrhoea
summary: Diarrhoea is loose, watery poo, usually caused by a stomach bug. In adults it normally gets better within 5 to 7 days.
redFlags: Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Bleeding from the bottom that is heavy or will not stop
Severe stomach pain or a hard, swollen stomach
Confusion, fainting or extreme drowsiness
Signs of sepsis such as cold, blotchy or blue-tinged skin, fast breathing or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it
urgentFlags: Bloody or black poo
Signs of dehydration such as dizziness, very dark urine or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Being unable to keep fluids down
Diarrhoea after recent travel abroad or a recent hospital stay or course of antibiotics
Diarrhoea with a weakened immune system, kidney disease or diabetes

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug (gastroenteritis)
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause; often with vomiting, cramps and a mild temperature.

commonCauses.title: Food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: Starts within hours to days of eating contaminated food.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Antibiotics and several other medicines can cause loose poo.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance or irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Diarrhoea that comes and goes may be linked to certain foods or IBS.

commonCauses.title: Inflammatory bowel disease
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, ongoing diarrhoea with blood or mucus can be due to Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.

selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids such as water in small sips; oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy helps replace lost salts
Eat when you feel able; plain foods are usually easiest
Wash your hands with soap and water after the toilet and before preparing food
Stay off work or school until 48 hours after the last episode
A pharmacist can advise if anti-diarrhoea medicine is suitable for you
avoid: Fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse
Anti-diarrhoea medicine if you have a high temperature or blood in your poo, unless a doctor advises it
Swimming pools for 2 weeks after the diarrhoea stops
seeDoctorIf: Diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days
Diarrhoea keeps coming back
You have lost weight without trying
Your bowel habits have changed for 3 weeks or more

name: Constipation
summary: Constipation means pooing less often than usual or having hard, difficult-to-pass poo. It is common and usually improves with more fibre, fluids and activity.
redFlags: Not passing any poo or wind at all, with a swollen stomach and vomiting
Severe stomach pain
Heavy bleeding from the bottom
urgentFlags: Constipation with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
Blood in your poo
Constipation with severe tiredness and weight loss

commonCauses.title: Not enough fibre or fluid
commonCauses.detail: A diet low in fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, or not drinking enough.

commonCauses.title: Lack of activity
commonCauses.detail: Sitting or lying down for long periods slows the bowel.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Strong painkillers, iron tablets and some other medicines commonly cause constipation.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy or changes in routine
commonCauses.detail: Hormone changes, travel or ignoring the urge to go.

commonCauses.title: Irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Constipation that alternates with diarrhoea and bloating.

selfCare: Gradually add more fibre such as fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrains
Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day
Be more active, even a daily walk can help
Go to the toilet when you feel the urge and resting your feet on a low stool can make pooing easier
Ask a pharmacist about laxatives if these changes do not help, following the pack instructions
avoid: Using laxatives every day for long periods without advice
Colon cleansing or 'detox' products, which are unproven
Ignoring the urge to poo
seeDoctorIf: You are not getting better with self-care
You are often constipated
You have a persistent change in bowel habit lasting 3 weeks or more
You have lost weight without trying, or feel tired all the time
You need to take laxatives regularly

name: Bloating
summary: Bloating is when your stomach feels full, tight or swollen. It is usually caused by wind or diet and often eases on its own.
redFlags: A swollen stomach with severe pain and being unable to pass poo or wind
Bloating with vomiting that will not stop
Vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like poo
urgentFlags: A stomach that is swollen and getting bigger quickly
Bloating with a high temperature or feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Wind and diet
commonCauses.detail: Beans, onions, fizzy drinks and swallowing air can all cause bloating.

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: Hard or infrequent poo often comes with bloating.

commonCauses.title: Irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Bloating that comes and goes with cramps and changes in bowel habit.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance
commonCauses.detail: For example lactose (milk sugar) or wheat intolerance.

commonCauses.title: Ovarian problems
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, bloating that is there most days can be a sign of ovarian cancer.

selfCare: Exercise regularly to help your bowel move
Eat smaller meals and eat slowly
Cut down on fizzy drinks, chewing gum and foods that give you wind
Keep a food diary to spot triggers
Ask a pharmacist about remedies for wind or constipation
avoid: Cutting out whole food groups without advice
Unproven 'detox' teas and supplements
seeDoctorIf: You have been bloated most days for 3 weeks or more
You have bloating that keeps coming back
You also have weight loss, blood in your poo or a change in bowel habit
You are over 50 and have new, persistent bloating

name: Farting and burping a lot
summary: Passing wind and burping are normal, but some foods and habits can make them happen more often. Changes to diet and eating habits usually help.
redFlags: Not passing any poo or wind at all, with a swollen stomach and vomiting
Severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Wind with blood in your poo
Wind with a high temperature and diarrhoea that is getting worse

commonCauses.title: Diet
commonCauses.detail: Beans, lentils, cabbage, onions, dried fruit and fizzy drinks produce more gas.

commonCauses.title: Swallowing air
commonCauses.detail: Eating quickly, chewing gum and smoking can make you swallow air.

commonCauses.title: Constipation or irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Both commonly cause trapped wind and bloating.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance
commonCauses.detail: For example lactose intolerance or coeliac disease.

selfCare: Eat smaller meals slowly and chew with your mouth closed
Cut down on foods that give you wind
Exercise regularly to help your digestion
Ask a pharmacist about remedies such as charcoal tablets or simeticone
avoid: Fizzy drinks, chewing gum and sucking sweets
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: Changes to your diet have not helped
You also have ongoing stomach pain, bloating or diarrhoea
You have lost weight without trying or noticed blood in your poo

name: Bleeding from the bottom
summary: Bright red blood on toilet paper is often caused by piles or a small tear, but blood in your poo should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Bleeding that is heavy or will not stop
Large amounts of blood or blood clots in the toilet
Bleeding with dizziness, fainting, a fast heartbeat or cold, clammy skin
Black, sticky, tar-like poo with feeling faint or unwell
Bleeding with severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Black or dark red poo
Bloody diarrhoea, especially with a high temperature
Bleeding that has lasted more than a day or two
Bleeding in a child

commonCauses.title: Piles (haemorrhoids)
commonCauses.detail: Bright red blood after pooing, sometimes with itching or a lump around the bottom.

commonCauses.title: Anal fissure
commonCauses.detail: A small tear in the skin of the bottom, causing sharp pain when pooing and bright red blood.

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: Some stomach bugs cause bloody diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Inflammatory bowel disease
commonCauses.detail: Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis can cause blood and mucus with diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Bowel polyps or cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason any blood in poo should be checked, especially if you are older or your bowel habits have changed.

selfCare: Eat more fibre and drink plenty of fluids to keep poo soft
Do not strain on the toilet
Gently pat the area clean with moist toilet paper
Ask a pharmacist about creams for piles if that is the likely cause, while waiting to see a doctor
avoid: Assuming bleeding is piles without being checked
Pushing or straining when pooing
Ignoring bleeding because it has stopped
seeDoctorIf: You have any blood in your poo, even once, that has not been checked
You have a change in bowel habits lasting 3 weeks or more
You have lost weight without trying or feel very tired
You have a lump in or around your bottom

name: Black or very dark poo
summary: Iron tablets, bismuth stomach medicines and some foods can turn poo black. Black, sticky, tar-like poo can also mean bleeding in the stomach and must be checked quickly.
redFlags: Black, sticky, tar-like poo with dizziness, fainting, a fast heartbeat or cold, clammy skin
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Black poo with severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Black, sticky or tar-like poo that is not explained by iron tablets, bismuth medicines or food
Black poo with stomach pain or indigestion
Black poo while taking blood thinners or anti-inflammatory painkillers

commonCauses.title: Iron tablets or bismuth medicines
commonCauses.detail: These commonly turn poo dark green or black and are harmless in that case.

commonCauses.title: Foods
commonCauses.detail: Black liquorice, blueberries and beetroot can darken poo.

commonCauses.title: Bleeding in the stomach or upper bowel
commonCauses.detail: A stomach ulcer or inflamed stomach lining can bleed, giving sticky, tar-like black poo.

selfCare: Check whether you have recently started iron tablets, bismuth medicines or eaten dark foods
If none of these explain it, get medical advice the same day
Keep a note of any medicines you take, including painkillers, to tell the doctor
avoid: Taking anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin until you have been checked
Waiting to see if unexplained black, sticky poo goes away
Alcohol until you have been checked
seeDoctorIf: Your poo stays dark and you are unsure why
You feel tired and look pale
You have ongoing indigestion or stomach pain

name: Change in bowel habits
summary: A change in how often you poo or what it looks like that lasts for weeks is worth getting checked. Most causes are not serious, but it can be an early sign of bowel cancer.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding from the bottom
Not passing any poo or wind at all, with a swollen stomach and vomiting
Severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Black, sticky, tar-like poo
Bloody diarrhoea with a high temperature
Feeling very unwell with ongoing diarrhoea

commonCauses.title: Diet or lifestyle changes
commonCauses.detail: Changes in food, fluids, activity or stress can alter bowel habits for a while.

commonCauses.title: Irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Diarrhoea, constipation or both, with cramps and bloating that come and go.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: New medicines can cause constipation or diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease
commonCauses.detail: Ongoing diarrhoea, weight loss or blood and mucus need tests.

commonCauses.title: Bowel cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason a persistent change, especially with blood or weight loss, should be checked.

selfCare: Keep a diary of your bowel habits, diet and any symptoms to show the doctor
Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fibre and drink enough fluids
Take part in bowel cancer screening when invited
avoid: Waiting months to see if a persistent change settles
Self-treating with laxatives or anti-diarrhoea medicines for weeks without advice
seeDoctorIf: A change in bowel habits has lasted 3 weeks or more
You have blood in your poo
You have lost weight without trying
You have a lump in your stomach or bottom, or feel very tired for no reason

name: Itchy bottom
summary: An itchy bottom is common and often caused by sweating, irritation from soaps or wiping, piles or threadworms. It usually improves with simple hygiene measures.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding from the bottom that will not stop
urgentFlags: Itching with a painful, hot, swollen lump near the bottom and a high temperature
Bleeding from the bottom with a change in bowel habits

commonCauses.title: Skin irritation
commonCauses.detail: Sweating, scented soaps, wet wipes or wiping too hard.

commonCauses.title: Threadworms
commonCauses.detail: Very common in children and families; itching is usually worse at night.

commonCauses.title: Piles or a small tear
commonCauses.detail: Piles and anal fissures can cause itching as well as bleeding or pain.

commonCauses.title: Skin conditions or thrush
commonCauses.detail: Eczema, psoriasis or a fungal infection can affect the skin around the bottom.

selfCare: Wash the area with water and pat dry gently after pooing
Use plain, unperfumed soap and wear loose cotton underwear
Try not to scratch; keep nails short
Ask a pharmacist about treatment for threadworms or soothing creams if the cause seems clear
avoid: Scented soaps, bubble bath and wet wipes
Scratching, which damages the skin and makes itching worse
Using steroid creams for long periods without advice
seeDoctorIf: Itching has not improved after a few weeks of self-care
You have a lump in or around your bottom
You have bleeding or a change in bowel habits
It keeps coming back

name: Pain or a lump in the bottom
summary: Pain around the bottom is often due to piles or a small tear in the skin, and these usually get better with soft poo and simple care.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding from the bottom that will not stop
Severe pain with a high temperature, feeling very unwell, and spreading redness around the bottom or groin
urgentFlags: A painful, hot, swollen lump near the bottom, especially with a high temperature
Severe pain that stops you sitting or walking
A pile that is very painful and has turned purple or cannot be pushed back

commonCauses.title: Piles (haemorrhoids)
commonCauses.detail: Swollen blood vessels in and around the bottom, causing lumps, itching and bleeding.

commonCauses.title: Anal fissure
commonCauses.detail: A small tear causing sharp pain during and after pooing.

commonCauses.title: Anal abscess
commonCauses.detail: A painful collection of pus near the bottom that usually needs draining.

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: Straining with hard poo can cause or worsen pain.

selfCare: Keep poo soft with more fibre and fluids
Do not strain and do not delay when you need to go
A warm bath can ease pain and itching
Paracetamol can help with pain, following the pack instructions
Ask a pharmacist about creams for piles
avoid: Straining on the toilet or sitting on it for long periods
Painkillers containing codeine, which can cause constipation
Scented wipes or soaps around the bottom
seeDoctorIf: Pain has not improved after 7 days of self-care
You have blood in your poo that has not been checked
You have a lump that does not go away
Your symptoms keep coming back

name: Loss of appetite
summary: Losing your appetite for a few days is common during an illness, with stress or after starting a medicine. If it lasts or comes with weight loss, it should be checked.
redFlags: Not eating or drinking at all with confusion, extreme drowsiness or fainting
Vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like poo
urgentFlags: Not being able to keep fluids down
Signs of dehydration such as very dark urine or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes

commonCauses.title: Short-term illness
commonCauses.detail: Infections such as colds, flu or stomach bugs often reduce appetite for a few days.

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or low mood
commonCauses.detail: Emotional strain commonly affects appetite.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines can reduce appetite or change taste.

commonCauses.title: Longer-term conditions
commonCauses.detail: Thyroid, liver, kidney or bowel problems and some cancers can cause ongoing appetite loss.

selfCare: Eat small, frequent meals or snacks rather than large meals
Choose foods you enjoy and that are easy to eat
Keep drinking fluids even if you do not feel like eating
Light activity and fresh air can help stimulate appetite
avoid: Skipping fluids along with food
Appetite-boosting supplements sold online, which are often unproven
seeDoctorIf: Your appetite has not returned after 2 weeks
You are losing weight without trying
You also feel low, anxious or hopeless
You have other ongoing symptoms such as tiredness, pain or night sweats

name: Lump in the groin or tummy (hernia)
summary: A soft lump in the groin or near the belly button that gets bigger when you cough or strain is often a hernia. Most are not urgent but should be checked.
redFlags: A hernia or groin lump that is suddenly very painful, hard or cannot be pushed back
A painful lump with vomiting and being unable to poo or pass wind
A lump that has turned red, purple or dark
urgentFlags: A groin lump with a high temperature and tenderness
A lump that is becoming more painful
A painful lump or swelling in the scrotum

commonCauses.title: Inguinal hernia
commonCauses.detail: Part of the bowel or fat pushes through a weak spot in the groin; more common in men.

commonCauses.title: Umbilical or incisional hernia
commonCauses.detail: A bulge at the belly button or near a previous operation scar.

commonCauses.title: Swollen lymph glands
commonCauses.detail: Glands in the groin can swell with an infection in the leg, foot or genitals.

commonCauses.title: Skin lumps
commonCauses.detail: Cysts or lipomas (fatty lumps) under the skin.

selfCare: Avoid heavy lifting and straining until the lump has been checked
Keep poo soft to avoid straining
Note whether the lump disappears when you lie down
avoid: Forcing a lump back in if it is painful
Relying on a support belt instead of getting it checked
seeDoctorIf: You have a new lump in your groin or tummy
A lump gets bigger over time
A lump causes discomfort when you lift, cough or strain
